segments: First read Quadlet Service Lifecycle for generation, loading, startup, logs, persistence, and boot-time requirements. This article provides in-depth examples of Pods and complete multi-service configurations.
Reference a Pod in a .container file:
A multi-container application: database, API, and proxy
This example uses an Nginx reverse proxy + Python API + PostgreSQL.

These code blocks represent separate files. The image registry.example.com/demo/myapi:latest is a nonfunctional placeholder that must be replaced; the API image must provide curl, a health endpoint, and database connection retries. Prepare the Nginx configuration file yourself, pointing its upstream to app-api:3000; the example does not present an unspecified application as a ready-to-deploy product. EnvironmentFile must exist, have restricted permissions, and contain variables only in the application’s required format. Keep it out of git/the Nix store; environment variables themselves can also be read by processes with permission to inspect them.

.volume references give data an independent lifecycle, while .network provides name resolution. Use SELinux’s Z only for dedicated directories. Pod files suit containers that need to share localhost; do not mechanically mix them into an existing bridge-based multi-service design, since containers in the same Pod share ports and can conflict. HealthCmd runs inside the container, and Notify=healthy requires support in the installed version; design application readiness and ongoing health recovery separately.
For automatic updates, linger, generator checks, and service removal, refer to the lifecycle article. Do not run enable on generated services.
